content.text: Inheritance is a fundamental concept in object-oriented programming that allows a new class (subclass) to inherit properties and behaviors (fields and methods) from an existing class (superclass). It promotes code reusability and supports the "is-a" relationship.

items: Superclass (Parent Class): The class that provides the common properties and behaviors (e.g., Loan class).
Subclass (Child Class): The class that inherits properties and behaviors from the superclass (e.g., HomeLoan, VehicleLoan).
"is-a" relationship: The subclass is a specialized version of the superclass. For example, VehicleLoan is a Loan.
Reusability: Subclasses inherit the attributes and methods of the superclass, so you don’t need to rewrite common code.
Extensibility: You can extend the functionality of the superclass by adding new features or modifying existing ones in the subclass.
Maintainability: Changes in the superclass are automatically inherited by the subclasses, reducing redundancy.
Single-Level Inheritance: A subclass directly inherits from a superclass.
Multi-Level Inheritance: A subclass inherits from another subclass, which in turn inherits from a superclass.
Java does not support Multiple Inheritance: A subclass cannot inherit from more than one superclass.
The subclass inherits all non-private fields and methods from the superclass.
If a subclass object is created, it has access to both the subclass's own members and the inherited ones from the superclass.
The extends keyword is used to define inheritance in Java.
Multi-Level Inheritance is a chain of inheritance where a class is derived from another class, which itself is derived from another class.
When an object of a subclass is created, the constructor of the superclass is executed first, followed by the subclass constructor.
This is called constructor chaining.

Single Responsibility Principle (SRP): A class should have only one reason to change. Inheritance should be used to represent common features shared between classes, not to bundle unrelated functionalities.

Encapsulation: Even though inheritance allows access to superclass members, it is still a good practice to keep instance variables of the superclass private and access them via getter and setter methods.
Avoid Multiple Inheritance: Since Java doesn’t support multiple inheritance (due to the diamond problem), use interfaces or composition to achieve the same effect.
Java supports single-level and multi-level inheritance but does not support multiple inheritance due to potential issues like the diamond problem.
You can use constructor chaining in inheritance to ensure that the constructor of the superclass is invoked before the subclass constructor.
Reusability and extensibility are the key benefits of using inheritance.
